newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian kerosene players bet on outcome of winter.
newsitem.headline: Asian kerosene players bet on outcome of winter.

text.p: Buyers and sellers of kerosene are gambling big on the North Asian winter in the build up to the peak demand fourth quarter, traders said on Friday.

Consumers banking on a mild winter have held back on buying kerosene, used for heating and jet fuel, reckoning on buying cheaper later. Sellers counting on a severe winter are building stocks, they said.
No one is betting 100 percent on the winter weather, but sellers are counting on the absence of exports from the United States and seasonal demand to keep the market tight.
Buyers, who built up stocks over the summer, are hoping regional refinery expansions will tilt the supply balance in their favour.
Last year, the Japanese winter was very cold and the price of kerosene delivered there shot up to a record $37.00 per barrel.
Sellers are betting on that happening again and have up to 4.0 million barrels stockpiled in Abu Dhabi, Singapore and Guam, traders said.

Kerosene prices in Singapore, a benchmark for other regional markets, averaged $22.80 per barrel in 1995. But so far this year they have averaged $26.95 -- 18 percent higher. Prompt kerosene was assessed on Thursday at around $30.00 per barrel.
"We think its overpriced. It's too expensive to buy right now," one major Japanese importer said.
"We think the winter is not going to be so cold," he said in explaining why Japanese importers were not yet buying their winter stocks.
At this time last year, at least two major companies had signed up most of their winter requirements. This year, only one one company has partially covered its demand, traders said.
Japanese refiners are leaving their options open, either to import or produce more kerosene, depending which is more economical, a trader said.
Japan's reluctance to buy forward for the winter was also due to large purchases in the summer, traders said.

The country's July imports, at 149,000 kilolitres (kl), were double of those in July 1995 and boosted stocks at the end of July to 3.04 million kl. Stocks hit a record low in January at 2.65 million kl.
Last winter it imported 2,233,000 kl (14.045 million barrels) of kerosene between November 1995 and February 1996.

During the same period, South Korea imported 20.225 million barrels, but this year will import less as it has already secured 6.7 million barrels through term contracts and has expanded refining capacity, traders said.
By November, capacity will have been raised to 2.44 million barrels per day (bpd) from 1.82 million bpd in 1995 and some Korean refiners have become kerosene exporters, traders said.

"Korean refiners have already signed contracts to supply jet (kerosene) to Japan for the winter. They will have more products to export once two new crude units start up later this year," a Japanese enduser said.
But sellers are not deterred.
"Whether the winter is mild or cold, Japan would still need to import," one trader said.
The absence of exports from the United States, a major seller last winter, is expected to keep the Asian market tight, he said.
U.S. distillate stocks, which include jet, are more than 20 million barrels down over the same time last year, which is likely to limit U.S. exports severely, he said.
